title: Before the loss
hookLine: grief can begin before a death, while caring for someone

cards: Sunday night. A daughter sits at the kitchen table filling her mother's pill organizer, the way she has for months. Her mother is still here, in the next room, laughing at a game show.

And the daughter is already grieving. Not for the woman in the next room, exactly, but for the one who used to drive, who remembered every birthday, who used to fill her own pills and would have hated needing help.
Nobody sends flowers for that. There's no service for a loss that's still happening, one small piece at a time.

teach.b: First, a name for it. The psychiatrist Erich Lindemann wrote about anticipatory grief: mourning that begins before a death, when a death is expected.
People caring for someone with a long illness describe it as losing things one at a time: a shared joke the other person can't follow anymore, a role, a plan for later, the future they pictured.

Carers describe love and tiredness side by side, sometimes a wish for the struggle to be over, and then guilt for having wished it. All of that can be in one heart in one evening. None of it cancels the love.
Third, an old story of grief before and after. In the second book of Samuel, King David's young child falls ill.

David fasts and lies all night on the ground. When the child dies, his servants are afraid to tell him. But David sees them whispering, understands, then gets up, washes, changes his clothes, and eats.
Asked why, he says: "While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept," and then, "can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me."
His grief before looked one way, and his grief after another. Fourth, a caution. Grieving before a death doesn't mean the grief is used up when the death comes.
Some find the after easier, some harder, some just different.

how: Hospice teams and carers' support groups talk openly about anticipatory grief, and friends can help most with practical things: meals, errands, or a few hours of respite care.

games.q: you're one of David's servants. the child has died, and you're afraid to tell the king. what does David do?
o: he tears his clothes and refuses all food from then on.
he sees you whispering, understands, then rises, washes and eats.

games.why: David rises, washes and eats: "can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me."

practice: Bring to mind someone caring for another person, a parent looking after a parent, someone nursing a partner, a friend with a sick child, or yourself, if the carer is you.
Hold them in mind with no advice attached, just seeing them at the end of a long day.
Then let one small kindness for them take shape, a message that needs no reply, a meal left at the door, an hour of sitting in so they can rest, and if you're the carer, let the kindness be for you.

wordCard.voice: Anticipatory grief, Erich Lindemann's name for mourning that begins before a death, as a carer loses things one at a time. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: before and after. Love and tiredness can share one heart in one evening. Until tomorrow.
